## Hands-on 4 – Exploring the menu {#hands-on-4-work-the-menu .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 4 is exploratory.** Try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which decisions move the estimate.

1. Start from the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR, which every argument of `try_spec()` takes as its default
2. Change **one decision** in `try_spec()` and read what happens to *b*, the partial *r*, the CR2 p and the placement; `my_experiments()` lists every try
3. Do it again with a different decision. Three or four is plenty, and one option that is off the curve, to read why it is refused
4. Then rerun the one you can argue for best with `try_spec()`, so that it is your last try, and **submit it** with `submit_exploration()`
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your dot appears on the live **Multiverse** page within seconds, and we read the dots from the whole class once everyone has submitted.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is **not** your preregistered analysis. You are allowed to look, change your mind and try again, which is why this phase has a name of its own.
:::

::: notes
Right. This is where you get your hands properly dirty, and I want to be explicit about what kind of activity it is, because it differs from the preregistered analysis that comes later. Task four is exploration. Start from the reproduced specification, my own model, which every argument of try underscore spec takes as its default, whichever analyst you reproduced. Change one decision with try underscore spec, and look at what happens to the coefficient, the partial r, the CR2 p-value and the placement among the eight hundred and sixty-four. Every try is logged, and my underscore experiments lists them for you. Then do it again with a different decision – three or four goes is plenty. Ask for one option that is off the curve as well, such as pooled OLS or a weight by population, and read the reason that comes back with the refusal. Then rerun whichever one you can argue for best with try underscore spec, so that it is your last try, and submit it with submit underscore exploration, which sends whatever you tried last. Your dot appears on the live multiverse page within seconds. Once everyone has submitted, we read what the class built. The second fragment matters: this is not your preregistered analysis. Here you are allowed to look, change your mind and try again. Most published work never says that such a phase took place, which is why this one has a name of its own.
:::

## Fitting and download times {#how-long-will-anything-take .smaller visibility="hidden"}

::: {.small}
Measured on the 270-row panel, on an ordinary laptop:

| What | Time |
|---|---|
| `feols`, two-way or country fixed effects | under 0.01 s |
| `try_spec()` in the workspace, with its CR2 test | about 1 s for the first call, which loads the packages, and under 0.1 s after it |
| `try_spec()` in the browser lab | instant: it reads the curve that ships with the page |
:::

::: {.small}
**Every fit is fast.** A participant who is waiting is waiting for a package **download**:

- browser lab: its packages, **≈ 24 MB**, once when the page opens, a long moment on poor wifi. Nothing after that: the Task 2 graph reads its adjustment sets from a table that ships with the page
- the workspace, first run: the whole package set installs once
:::

::: notes
[Facilitator slide, hidden in the deck – for answering "how long should this take?" without guessing.] Every fit on this panel is effectively instantaneous, and so is the CR2 test that classes it: the workspace fits each specification live and computes its clustered errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom in a tenth of a second, the first call being the slowest because it loads the packages. Nobody is waiting for a model. What people do wait for is a package download. The browser lab downloads its packages, about twenty-four megabytes, once when the page opens, which is a long moment on a bad connection. After that it reads every result from files that ship with the page, the curve for the menu and a table of the answers of dagitty for the graph of Task 2, so nothing else triggers a download there. The first run in the workspace installs the whole set once. So if someone reports that it is stuck, ask what it is stuck on before assuming the model is the problem.
:::
